message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"2094c811e40e88f776c5f0df22856ee7e7efa396e48b94d7aaa7338ad62526ad","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tx-class-c:lineage:70","source_registry_sha256":"73669019241a96617275447ad5e45b56c17a2d4bd395699448d85850cfc5bafb","units":[{"unit_id":"sec13-u01","module_id":"sec13-m01","objective_ids":["sec13-u01"],"title":{"text":"Bicycles are vehicles","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Texas treats a bicycle as a vehicle, so a rider has the same rights and duties as any vehicle driver.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01"]},{"text":"Traffic offenses on a bicycle draw the same penalties as in a motor vehicle and go on the rider's driver record.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Eli rides his bicycle through a red light on an empty street and is cited.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F03"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Riders halt at each red light, and a bicycle violation draws the same penalty as in a motor vehicle, recorded on the driver record.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F02"]},"result":{"text":"Eli faces the same penalty a driver would, and the conviction goes on his driver record.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking riding against traffic is safer because the rider can see cars coming.","fact_ids":["sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},"correction":{"text":"Riders always travel with the flow of traffic and never ride against it.","fact_ids":["sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Same road, same rules.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A friend says bicycle tickets do not count on a driver record. Is that right?","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]},"answer":{"text":"No. Every traffic conviction goes on the rider's driver record.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]},"rationale":{"text":"A bicycle violation draws the same penalty as in a motor vehicle, and every traffic conviction goes on the driver record no matter which one was operated.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Riding as a vehicle","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"A bicycle is a vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},{"text":"Same rules, same penalties.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson opens the section on bicycle laws and safety. The starting point is simple: Texas treats a bicycle as a vehicle. We will look at the rights and duties a rider shares with every vehicle driver, the one exception the handbook allows, the penalties for breaking a traffic law on a bicycle, where those convictions are recorded, the duty to obey every traffic law, sign, and signal, and the rule about which direction a rider travels on the road. A rider holds the same rights and owes the same duties as any vehicle driver.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Same rights, same penalties","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Same rights and duties as drivers.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02"]},{"text":"Except rules that cannot fit a bicycle.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02"]},{"text":"Same penalties; same driver record.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Texas treats a bicycle as a vehicle. A rider holds the same rights and owes the same duties as any vehicle driver, except where a rule by its nature cannot fit a bicycle. Breaking a traffic law on a bicycle draws the same penalty as breaking it in a motor vehicle. Every traffic conviction goes on the person's driver record, no matter whether they were riding a bicycle or driving a motor vehicle at the time. So a ticket on a bicycle is not a lesser matter. It carries the same penalty and lands on the same driver record as a ticket earned behind the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Signals and direction","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Obey every law, sign, and signal.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"Stop at every stop sign and red light.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"Always ride with traffic.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Riders obey every traffic law, sign, and signal. That includes coming to a stop at each stop sign and each red light, just as a driver would. Riders always travel with the flow of traffic and never ride against it. These two rules, obeying every signal and riding with the flow, are the basics that every other bicycle rule builds on. So a rider who runs a red light or rides against traffic is breaking the same rules a driver would. Riders halt at each stop sign and red light, and they always travel with the flow of traffic.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"With traffic, not against","fact_ids":["sec13-R01","sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Ride with the flow of traffic.","fact_ids":["sec13-R01","sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]},{"text":"Never ride against it.","fact_ids":["sec13-R01","sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]},{"text":"Stop at every red light.","fact_ids":["sec13-R01","sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from a common belief. Some people think riding against traffic is safer, because the rider can see the cars that are coming. The handbook says riders always travel with the flow of traffic and never ride against it. A second trap is about signals. Some riders treat red lights and stop signs as optional when the road is empty. They are not. Riders halt at each stop sign and red light. When a question describes a rider's direction or behavior at a signal, apply the same rule you would apply to any vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec13-R01","sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the driver record","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"A bicycle ticket.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]},{"text":"Does it count?","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a friend says bicycle tickets do not count on a person's driver record. Is that right? Work out your answer before reading on. No, it is not. Every traffic conviction goes on the driver record, no matter whether the person was riding a bicycle or driving a motor vehicle. A violation on a bicycle also draws the same penalty as the same violation in a motor vehicle. That follows from the starting rule: Texas treats a bicycle as a vehicle, with the same rights and duties as any vehicle driver. Same penalties apply.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Bicycles as vehicles in brief","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"A bicycle is a vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"Same penalties, same record.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"Obey signals; ride with traffic.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Texas treats a bicycle as a vehicle, so a rider holds the same rights and owes the same duties as any vehicle driver, except where a rule cannot by its nature fit a bicycle. Breaking a traffic law on a bicycle draws the same penalty as in a motor vehicle, and every traffic conviction goes on the driver record, whatever the person was operating. Riders obey every traffic law, sign, and signal, halting at each stop sign and red light, and they always travel with the flow of traffic, never against it. Next, where riders position themselves on the road.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec13-u02","module_id":"sec13-m02","objective_ids":["sec13-u02"],"title":{"text":"Lane position and sharing","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},"why_how":[{"text":"A rider moving slower than traffic keeps as close as possible to the right curb or edge, with listed exceptions.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Riders may use the shoulder, may ride two abreast within one lane, and are guided by shared lane markings.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Mae rides slower than traffic on a two-way street and sees parked cars and debris ahead near the curb.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Slower riders keep right except when passing, preparing a left turn, avoiding hazards such as parked cars or debris, or riding an outside lane too narrow to share.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},"result":{"text":"Mae moves away from the curb to avoid the parked cars and debris, then returns to the right edge.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a rider must always stay at the right edge, whatever the road.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-F06","sec13-R02"]},"correction":{"text":"On a one-way road with two or more marked lanes, a rider keeps as close as possible to the left curb or edge, and slower riders elsewhere have listed exceptions to keeping right.","fact_ids":["sec13-R02","sec13-F06","sec13-F10"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Right when slower, left on one-way.","fact_ids":["sec13-R02"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Two friends want to ride side by side on a road with lanes. What is the rule?","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-R05"]},"answer":{"text":"They share one lane and must not block traffic.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"Two riders side by side share one lane without blocking cars; riders may also use the shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec13-R05","sec13-F07","sec13-F08"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Where riders belong","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F10","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right edge, left edge.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F10","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13"]},{"text":"Pairs, shoulders, and markings.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F10","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers where a bicycle rider belongs on the road. The answer depends on the road and on how fast the rider is moving compared with traffic. We will look at the rule for riders moving slower than traffic, the listed exceptions that let a rider move away from the right edge, the special rule for one-way roads with two or more marked lanes, how two riders may ride side by side, the use of road shoulders, and what shared lane markings painted on the road tell riders and drivers. Pairs share one lane, and shoulders are allowed.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F10","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Keeping right when slower","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slower riders keep near the right edge.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Except passing or turning left.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Except hazards or narrow lanes.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"A rider moving slower than the surrounding traffic stays as close as possible to the right curb or edge. There are exceptions. The rider may move away from the right edge when passing another vehicle, when preparing to turn left, when avoiding hazards such as parked cars or debris, or when riding in an outside lane narrower than fourteen feet or too narrow for a bicycle and a car to travel side by side. So keeping right is the general rule for a slower rider, and each of the listed exceptions gives the rider a reason to take more of the lane.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"One-way roads and the left edge","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"One-way, two or more marked lanes.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]},{"text":"Keep near the left curb or edge.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]},{"text":"Different from the right-edge rule.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"On a one-way road with at least two marked lanes, a rider keeps as close as possible to the left curb or edge. This is a different rule from the one for slower riders on other roads, who keep near the right curb or edge. So the road type changes the edge. A one-way road with two or more marked lanes points the rider toward the left edge. A rider moving slower than traffic elsewhere keeps toward the right edge, with the listed exceptions for passing, left turns, hazards, and lanes that are too narrow to share safely with a car.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pairs, shoulders, and markings","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two abreast share one lane.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]},{"text":"Shoulders may be used.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]},{"text":"Markings show rider position.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two riders riding side by side on a road with lanes share one lane, and they must not block the movement of traffic. Riders are allowed to use the shoulder of the road. Shared lane markings, painted in the lane, help riders position themselves away from car doors that may open and in lanes too narrow to share. They also show other road users where riders are likely to be, promote safe passing, and discourage riding the wrong way. So the shoulder, a shared lane for pairs, and the painted markings all help riders and drivers share the road.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Left edge or right edge","fact_ids":["sec13-R02","sec13-F06","sec13-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"One-way, two-plus lanes: left edge.","fact_ids":["sec13-R02","sec13-F06","sec13-F10"]},{"text":"Slower than traffic: right edge.","fact_ids":["sec13-R02","sec13-F06","sec13-F10"]},{"text":"Exceptions let riders move out.","fact_ids":["sec13-R02","sec13-F06","sec13-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the two edge rules. Learners often think a rider always keeps to the right edge. On a one-way road with at least two marked lanes, the rider keeps as close as possible to the left curb or edge instead. On other roads, a rider moving slower than traffic keeps as close as possible to the right curb or edge, except when passing, preparing a left turn, avoiding hazards, or riding an outside lane too narrow to share. When a question describes a rider's position, check the road type first, then whether an exception applies.","fact_ids":["sec13-R02","sec13-F06","sec13-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the side-by-side rule","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-R05","sec13-F08","sec13-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two friends, side by side.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-R05","sec13-F08","sec13-F13"]},{"text":"What is the rule?","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-R05","sec13-F08","sec13-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: two friends want to ride side by side on a road with marked lanes. What is the rule? Work out your answer before reading on. They may ride side by side, but they share one lane and must not block the movement of traffic. Riders may also use the shoulder of the road. And shared lane markings show where riders are likely to be, help riders stay away from opening car doors, and discourage wrong-way riding. Each of these rules is about sharing the road without blocking it. Pairs must not block traffic.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-R05","sec13-F08","sec13-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Lane position in brief","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slower riders keep right, with exceptions.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]},{"text":"One-way multilane: keep left.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]},{"text":"Pairs share one lane; shoulders allowed.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, a rider moving slower than traffic keeps as close as possible to the right curb or edge, except when passing, preparing a left turn, avoiding hazards such as parked cars or debris, or riding an outside lane narrower than fourteen feet or too tight to share. On a one-way road with two or more marked lanes, a rider keeps as close as possible to the left curb or edge. Two riders side by side share one lane without blocking traffic, riders may use the shoulder, and shared lane markings guide position and promote safe passing. Next, arm signals and rider conduct.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-F06","sec13-R02","sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F13","sec13-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec13-u03","module_id":"sec13-m03","objective_ids":["sec13-u03"],"title":{"text":"Arm signals and conduct","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03","sec13-F05"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Riders signal right turns, left turns, and stops with their arms.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]},{"text":"Riders sit on a permanent seat, carry only as many people as the bicycle is built for, never hitch rides, and keep a hand on the bars.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-F11","sec13-F12","sec13-R04"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Ivy is about to turn left at a corner on her bicycle.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A left turn means the left arm held flat.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]},"result":{"text":"Ivy holds her left arm out flat before turning left.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a right turn must always be signaled with the right arm.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]},"correction":{"text":"A right turn means the left arm up or the right arm held flat; either is allowed.","fact_ids":["sec13-R03","sec13-F09"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Flat left, up right, down stop.","fact_ids":["sec13-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A rider wants to carry a large box that would take both hands to hold. Is that allowed?","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R04"]},"answer":{"text":"No. A rider must keep at least one hand on the handlebars.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12"]},"rationale":{"text":"A rider never carries an object that stops them from keeping at least one hand on the handlebars.","fact_ids":["sec13-R04","sec13-F12"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Signals and safe conduct","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F05","sec13-F11","sec13-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Arm signals for turns and stops.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F05","sec13-F11","sec13-F12"]},{"text":"Seats, hitching, and handlebars.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F05","sec13-F11","sec13-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers how riders signal and how they conduct themselves on the bicycle. Riders use arm signals to show right turns, left turns, and stops, and the handbook allows two different signals for a right turn. Then there are three conduct rules about the bicycle itself: where the rider sits and how many people may ride, the ban on hitching to moving vehicles, and the rule about carrying things while keeping a hand on the handlebars. A right turn is the left arm up or the right arm flat, a left turn is the left arm flat, and a stop is the left arm down.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F05","sec13-F11","sec13-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Arm signals","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right turn: left arm up or right arm flat.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]},{"text":"Left turn: left arm flat.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]},{"text":"Stop: left arm pointed down.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Riders signal with their arms. For a right turn, the rider either holds the left arm up or holds the right arm out flat. For a left turn, the rider holds the left arm out flat. For a stop, the rider points the left arm down. So the left arm does most of the work: up for a right turn, flat for a left turn, and down for a stop, with the right arm held flat as a second way to show a right turn. The right arm held flat is the only right-arm signal in the list. For the left arm, up is right, flat is left, and down is stop.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Seats and passengers","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sit on a permanent, regular seat.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R04"]},{"text":"No more riders than designed.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R04"]},{"text":"Same for every bicycle.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"A rider sits only on or astride a permanent, regular seat attached to the bicycle. A bicycle never carries more people than it was designed or equipped to hold. So a bicycle built for one carries one rider, sitting on its seat, and a bicycle built for two carries two. Riding on the handlebars or on a rack that is not a seat breaks the rule. These rules are about the bicycle itself, and they apply no matter where the bicycle is ridden on the road, on the shoulder, or in a lane shared with traffic going the same way.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Hitching and handlebars","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-F12","sec13-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Never hitch to a moving vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-F12","sec13-R04"]},{"text":"Keep at least one hand on the bars.","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-F12","sec13-R04"]},{"text":"No loads that take both hands.","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-F12","sec13-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"A rider never hitches the bicycle, or their own body, to a moving streetcar or vehicle on the road. A rider also never carries a package, bundle, or object that stops them from keeping at least one hand on the handlebars. Being pulled by a vehicle is never allowed, and any load must leave at least one hand free for the handlebars. Together with the seat and passenger rule, these make up the handbook's three conduct rules for the bicycle itself. And a rider sits only on a permanent, regular seat, carrying no more people than the bicycle was designed to hold.","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-F12","sec13-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two right-turn signals","fact_ids":["sec13-R03","sec13-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Left arm up: right turn.","fact_ids":["sec13-R03","sec13-F09"]},{"text":"Right arm flat: right turn.","fact_ids":["sec13-R03","sec13-F09"]},{"text":"Left arm flat: left turn.","fact_ids":["sec13-R03","sec13-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the arm signals. Learners often think a right turn must be signaled with the right arm. The handbook allows two signals for a right turn: the left arm held up, or the right arm held flat. A left turn is the left arm held flat, and a stop is the left arm pointed down. So the left arm held up and the left arm held flat mean different turns, and the left arm pointed down means a stop. When a question shows an arm position, match it carefully: up is right, flat is left, down is stop. Up, flat, down.","fact_ids":["sec13-R03","sec13-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the big box","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R04","sec13-F05","sec13-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"A load that needs both hands.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R04","sec13-F05","sec13-F11"]},{"text":"Allowed?","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R04","sec13-F05","sec13-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a rider wants to carry a large box that would take both hands to hold.
